title_ar: منبر الجمعة يستضيف الشيخ الددو محاضرا عن الظلم وعواقبه الوخيمة
title_en: The Friday Platform Hosts Sheikh al-Dedew Lecturing on Injustice and Its Grievous Consequences
body_ar:
ا ستضاف منبر الجمعة لهذا الأسبوع فضيلة الشيخ محمد الحسن ولد الددو، حيث ألقى فضيلته مساء اليوم 05 صفر 1433 هـ الموافق: 30/12/2011 محاضرة هامة عن الظلم خطره وعاقبته في المنبر الذي يقام أسبوعيا بمسجد الذكر بتنسويلم، وقد تحدث الشيخ في محاضرته عن الظلم وخطره وعقباته، بالإضافة إلى بعض الدروس المستفادة من الثروات العربية.

ووسط حضور كبير من طرف رواد العلم وطلبته، وجمهور عريض من ساكنة نواكشوط انطلق المنبر الذي أنعشه فضيلة الشيخ محمد الحسن ولد الددو، متحدثا عن الظلم وحكمه، ذاكرا بعض أنواعه وآثاره، وموقف الشرع في الرد على الظلم، مؤكدا على أن خطر المظالم يتعاظم مع كثرة المتضررين منها، وحسب المستويات التي تقع عليها، داعيا الأنظمة العربية التي لم تشملها الثورات بعد إلى ضرورة المبادرة وتبني الإصلاح والتغيير قبل أن يثور المظلومون وينهضوا لتغيير الوضع ببذل دمائهم كما حدث في أكثر من بلد عربي.

وأكد فضيلة الشيخ الددو أن الثورة حين تقوم تستهدف النظام القائم برمته والمؤسسة الدينية المرتبطة به بوصفها شريكا في الظلم و الفساد الذي تعانيه شعوبها، ومن الطبيعي أن يكون موقفها سلبيا من الثورة، بينما الواجب على العلماء والدعاة أن يكونوا مع أي دعوة لرفع الظلم وتغيير المنكر.

و شدد ولد الددو على أن من الواجب على الشعوب رفع الظلم و تغيير المنكر لأن البلد الذي يشيع فيه الفساد و الظلم و لا يوجد فيه من يرفع الظلم و ينكر المنكر يخشى عليه أن ينزل به عذاب يعمهم و لذلك تجب الهجرة منه.

وقال أيضا إن رفع الظلم واجب و إن الحاكم حين يظلم فردا واحدا من المجتمع فعلى الأمة رفع الظلم عنه وبالأحرى إذا كان المظلوم شعوب بأكملها كما هو حال الشعب الفلسطيني الذي يتعرض لأبشع أنواع التنكيل و القتل و التعذيب.

وأردف ولد الددو بأن الشعوب التي تثور لرفع الظلم لا يجوز لها الاستسلام بل يجب عليها أن تمضي حتى ترفع الظلم ومن مات من أبنائها فهو شهيد.

للمشاهدة اضغط هنا:
body_en:
The Friday platform this week hosted His Eminence Sheikh Muhammad al-Hasan Ould al-Dedew, His Eminence delivering on the evening of today, 05 Safar 1433 AH, corresponding to 30/12/2011, an important lecture on injustice — its danger and its outcome — at the platform held weekly at the Mosque of al-Dhikr in Tensoueilim. In his lecture the Sheikh spoke of injustice and its danger and its obstacles, besides some lessons drawn from the Arab riches.

Amid a large attendance of the leading figures of learning and their students, and a broad public from the residents of Nouakchott, the platform began, enlivened by His Eminence Sheikh Muhammad al-Hasan Ould al-Dedew, who spoke of injustice and of its ruling, mentioning some of its kinds and its effects, and the position of the Sharia in responding to injustice; affirming that the danger of injustices grows greater as those harmed by them grow more numerous, and according to the levels at which they occur; and calling on the Arab regimes not yet reached by the revolutions to the necessity of taking the initiative and adopting reform and change, before the wronged rise in revolt and stand up to change the situation at the cost of their blood, as has happened in more than one Arab country.

His Eminence Sheikh al-Dedew affirmed that a revolution, when it takes place, targets the standing regime in its entirety and the religious establishment bound up with it, as a partner in the injustice and corruption from which its peoples suffer; and that it is natural that the establishment's position towards the revolution should be a negative one, whereas what is obligatory (wājib) upon the scholars and the preachers is that they be with any call to lift injustice and to change wrong.

And Ould al-Dedew stressed that it is obligatory (wājib) upon peoples to lift injustice and to change wrong, because a country in which corruption and injustice become widespread, and in which there is no one to lift the injustice and reject the wrong, is to be feared for — lest a punishment descend upon it that engulfs them all; and for that reason migration from it is obligatory (wājib).

He also said that the lifting of injustice is obligatory (wājib), and that when the ruler wrongs a single individual of society it falls upon the community to lift the injustice from him — and all the more so when those wronged are entire peoples, as is the case with the Palestinian people, who are subjected to the most hideous kinds of brutalisation, killing and torture.

And Ould al-Dedew added that peoples who rise in revolt to lift injustice are not permitted (lā yajūz) to surrender, but rather that it is obligatory (wājib) upon them to press on until they lift the injustice; and whoever of their sons dies is a martyr.

flags.arabic: أن الشعوب التي تثور لرفع الظلم لا يجوز لها الاستسلام بل يجب عليها أن تمضي حتى ترفع الظلم ومن مات من أبنائها فهو شهيد / من الواجب على الشعوب رفع الظلم و تغيير المنكر … و لذلك تجب الهجرة منه
flags.context: the last four paragraphs of the record
options: translate faithfully and hold for an editorial decision
publish with a prominent editorial preface
flags.note: CRITICAL — the most editorially exposed record in this span, and editorial_review by a wide margin. In a journalist's summary, a named living scholar is reported as ruling: that it is obligatory upon peoples to remove injustice; that emigration from a country where injustice goes unchallenged is obligatory; that peoples who have risen in revolt are not permitted to surrender and must press on; and that those of them who die are martyrs. He is further reported as saying that revolutions rightly target the religious establishment as complicit. Whatever the Arabic context of December 2011, in English these are rulings that a reader can take as authorising continued armed revolt and as conferring the status of martyr on those killed in it. Publishing them in English carries legal as well as reputational exposure for the publisher in several Western jurisdictions, and consequences for the Sheikh in others. Nothing has been softened and nothing strengthened: the five-rulings mapping has been applied exactly, so واجب is 'obligatory' and لا يجوز is 'not permitted', and no qualification has been added that the record does not contain. The decision whether and how to publish belongs to Ummah Collective and the Sheikh's office and to no one else.

flags.arabic: بالإضافة إلى بعض الدروس المستفادة من الثروات العربية
flags.context: the last clause of the first paragraph
options: read as الثورات العربية ('the Arab revolutions')
translate literally as 'the Arab riches', as done here
mark the word as corrupt and give no rendering
flags.note: الثروات means 'riches' and makes no sense in a lecture about injustice. It is almost certainly a typing error for الثورات, 'the revolutions', which differs by one letter and which is the subject of every remaining paragraph of the record — the second paragraph names الثورات explicitly. The English nonetheless renders what the source says, per style guide section 11, so that the defect is visible rather than repaired out of sight. A reviewer should confirm from the recording and then the source should be corrected centrally, not here.

flags.arabic: عن الظلم خطره وعاقبته … عن الظلم وخطره وعقباته
flags.context: the two descriptions of the lecture's subject in the same paragraph
options: render each as it stands: 'its outcome' and then 'its obstacles'
read the second as عواقبه and render 'its consequences' both times
flags.note: The first phrase has عاقبته, 'its outcome'; the second has عقباته, 'its obstacles', where the sense plainly wants عواقبه, 'its consequences' — which is also what the record's own headline has. Both forms are rendered as they stand rather than harmonised, so that the reviewer sees there are three different words in the source for what is presumably one idea.

flags.arabic: متحدثا عن الظلم وحكمه … وموقف الشرع في الرد على الظلم … مذكرا بمراتب … وضوابط
flags.context: what the lecture covered, against what the record supplies
options: display with a prominent caveat that this is a journalist's summary and the reasoning is in the recording
display as a statement of his position
flags.note: critical_for_display. The record states that the Sheikh treated injustice 'and its ruling' and the position of the Sharia in responding to it, and then reports four rulings in a single sentence each, with none of the reasoning, none of the conditions, and none of the distinctions a jurist of his training would attach — most obviously on the obligation of emigration, which in the classical discussion is heavily qualified, and on who counts as a martyr. A reader takes what is here for his fatwa. It is not one: it is a report by a news desk of a lecture that exists as a recording at /index.php/fiker-islam.html?view=media&id=1590.

flags.arabic: ومن مات من أبنائها فهو شهيد
flags.context: the closing clause of the lecture summary
options: whoever of their sons dies is a martyr
whoever of their people is killed is a martyr
those of them who die are martyrs
flags.note: مات is 'dies', not 'is killed'; the Arabic does not restrict the statement to those killed in fighting, and the English must not narrow or widen it. أبناء is literally 'sons' and idiomatically the members of a people; the literal rendering is kept because the sentence is one whose exact scope a reviewing scholar will need to see. شهيد is rendered 'martyr', which is the established English, though the Arabic word is also 'witness' and the two senses are not separable in this literature.

translator_notes: This is a news report of a lecture, written by the site's news desk. Not a word of it is inside quotation marks, and every ruling in it is the reporter's compression of what the Sheikh said. The site must not render it as a fatwa.
The CMS timestamp is a bulk-upload date and is not evidence of when the report was written. The body's dates agree with each other and with the timestamp: 5 Safar 1433 was Friday 30 December 2011.

The ruling words here attach to acts of legally responsible persons — removing injustice, emigrating, surrendering — so they take the five-rulings mapping of style guide section 3. The kalām exemption of section 8 is not engaged; nothing in this record is a proposition about God.
واجب and يجب are rendered 'obligatory' uniformly, per the fixed mapping. The Sheikh is Maliki and the Hanafi farḍ/wājib distinction is not live here; no farḍ appears in the record.

لا يجوز is the negation of jāʾiz and is rendered 'not permitted', with the Arabic bracketed. It is a stronger statement than 'not advisable' and weaker than an explicit ḥarām, and the English should not be allowed to slide to either.
The first word of the body is broken across a space in the source (ا ستضاف for استضاف); preserved in body_ar.
منبر here is a recurring weekly public lecture, not the pulpit of a mosque; 'platform' is used and the mosque is named separately.
The closing 'to watch click here' is the site's navigation furniture; preserved in body_ar, recorded in source_download_link, omitted from body_en.
